title: Cell junction and nuclear forces as mediators of epithelial cell homeostasis
text:
In this basic research proposal, we will investigate how biophysical mechanisms, including mechanical forces
across epithelial cell-cell junctions and the nucleus, regulate the homeostasis of epithelial cells and tissues. A
better understanding of these processes will provide insight into epithelial tissue development, homeostasis,
and disease. Results from this study have the potential to identify new therapeutic targets for cancer, fibrosis,
wound healing, and chronic inflammation.

title: Architecture and Trajectory of Acquired Resistance to Therapy in AML
text:
Overall
The overall goal of this ARTNet Center is to understand the biological drivers of acquired drug resistance in
acute myeloid leukemia – an aggressive form of leukemia. We will employ novel experimental approaches,
advanced models, and a large biorepository of primary samples to study causes of resistance that are intrinsic
to the AML tumor cells as well as causes of resistance that are driven by the tumor cells interacting with their
local environment. This knowledge will be leveraged to identify and prioritize novel drug combination regimens
and translate these new therapeutic strategies into the clinics to prevent drug resistance and improve outcomes
for patients with AML.

title: Environmental chemicals impair epigenetic suppression of the endogenous retrovirus HML-2 in human primordial germ cells, predisposing the next generation to malignancies through HML-2 reactivation
text:
Millions of years ago, retroviruses infected ancient human ancestors and became a normal part of our genome
as Human Endogenous Retroviruses (HERVs). Although HERVs are generally suppressed in normal cells,
HML-2 is a special HERV species transiently activated in normal embryonic cells that are destined to produce
gametes as well as various adult-onset cancers, possibly contributing to formation of malignant cells. Taking
advantage of the latest advancement in modeling human embryos in cell cultures using cells not derived from
real human embryos, this project attempts to test the hypothesis that exposure of human embryos to
environmental toxic chemicals may cause incomplete suppression of HML-2 after their transient activation in
the gamete-producing cells and consequently increase the cancer risk in the next generation.

title: Mentoring patient-oriented research on point-of-care diagnostics for infectious diseases
text:
This midcareer investigator award in patient-oriented research is intended to provide the candidate, Dr. Paul
Drain, MD, MPH; Associate Professor at the University of Washington (UW), with protected time to develop a
structured and effective approach for research mentorship. His clinical research group has been conducting
diagnostic studies and clinical trials to advance rapid diagnostics and implementation science for the diagnosis
and treatment of infectious diseases, including HIV, tuberculosis (TB), and SARS-CoV-2. During this grant
period, Dr. Drain will provide mentorship and support for many students and trainees who seek to develop their
knowledge and skills in conducting patient-oriented research aimed at reducing sickness and deaths from
various infectious diseases of global importance.

title: Investigating splicing-derived antigens in the context of Rbm10-mutant lung adenocarcinoma
text:
Lung cancer is the leading global cause of cancer death but can be cured when treated with immunotherapy.
Specific genetic changes may make lung cancer more vulnerable to immunotherapy. This work aims to
understand susceptibility to immunotherapy in the 10% of lung adenocarcinomas that have one particular
genetic change, which causes loss of the protein RBM10.

title: Biomolecular Mass Spectrometry Core
text: BIOMOLECULAR MASS SPECTROMETRY CORE (BMSC): ABSTRACT The Biomolecular Mass Spectrometry Core (BMSC) is a key component of exposure assessment in the Center of Excellence in Environmental Toxicology (CEET) described in the Strategic Vision. The mission of the Core is to foster the use of biomolecular mass spectrometry to measure reporters of the exposome, (e.g., proteome, lipidome, metabolome and adductome) as biomarkers of exposure, adverse response, outcome and therapeutic response for diseases of environmental etiology. It performs work in cell-culture based models, in animal models and patient cohort studies designed in the Translational Research Support Core (TRSC). The BMSC recognizes the need to relate phenotypic changes in biomarkers with either changes in the transcriptome or with genetic variants and this is achieved by data integration performed by the Environmental Health Informatics Core (EHIC). The integration of genomic data and reporters of exposomic biomarkers offers the promise to deliver multi-omics approaches to diagnosis and prognosis. The BMSC is equipped with state-of-the-art ultraperformance liquid chromatography (UPLC)-MS and UPLC-high resolution (HR) MS instrumentation. It is also equipped with an ionchromatography system coupled to inductively coupled plasma (ICP)-MS for heavy metal analysis with speciation. In the Core untargeted approaches are followed by targeted LC-MS assays. Our targeted LC-MS assays use stable-isotope dilution (SID) LC-MS as the gold standard for precision and accuracy; many of the assays cannot be performed elsewhere in the world. The BMSC will achieve the CEET mission under the following aims: Aim 1: We will support the CEET thematic areas (Air Pollution & Lung Health; Environmental Exposures & Cancer; Windows-of- Susceptibility; and Environmental Neuroscience) and the cross-cutting theme of the effects of extreme weather on health with high-throughput services and facilitate biomarker discovery using Exposomics approaches (proteomics, lipidomics, metabolomics and adductomics). We will also support large multi-investigator grant applications, transcending CEET thematic areas. Aim 2: We will provide CEET investigators with highly sensitive and specific assays to quantify biomarkers of exposure and effect in model systems and in biofluids from population cohorts and patients. Aim 3: We will develop new assays for the thematic areas and prioritize services based on the needs of CEET investigators. Aim 4: We will provide analytical support for pilot project recipients, for preliminary studies in environmental health sciences and provide support for adjunct faculty with NIEHS funding from other universities in our area and from other Environmental Health Sciences Core Centers (EHS CCs) that do not have access to our assays. Aim 5: We will provide access and training to use state-of-the-art analytical equipment and software, for CEET investigators and their trainees, through monthly training sessions and annual workshops.

title: Interpretable Deep Forecasting of Hazardous Substance Use during High School
text:
PROJECT NARATIVE
20 million Americans battle with substance use disorder, typically initiated during adolescence. This project will
derive risk scores forecasting hazardous substance use in high school students through complex analyses of
brain imaging, demographic, health, and cognitive test data. The proposed novel analysis will use two large,
longitudinal, publicly-available datasets (National Consortium on Alcohol and Neurodevelopment in
Adolescence and Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development) and if our forecasting is accurate, future studies
can assess the potential of the risk scores for enhancing preventative care within precision medicine settings.

title: A Clinical Indications Prediction (CLIP) Scale for Human Mesenchymal Stem Cells
text:
Despite extensive clinical testing, mesenchymal stem/stromal cell (MSC)-based therapies continue to yield
suboptimal patient outcomes due to knowledge gaps in quality attributes that confer therapeutic efficacy, which
explains why most clinical studies produce MSCs using similar donor selection and manufacturing processes to
treat medically unrelated diseases. To address this problem, we developed a CLinical Indications Prediction
(CLIP) scale that predicts inter-donor differences in MSC potency for a range of clinically relevant activities.
Building on this discovery, in this proposal we propose to use the CLIP scale to interrogate how donor selection
and academic and industry-based manufacturing platforms impact MSC product potency and use this
information to produce products of defined potency that are tailored for specific disease indications to enhance
their efficacy.

title: Personalized Outreach and Multifaceted Interventions for Screening Enhancement (PROMISE) for Anal and Cervical Cancer Prevention and Treatment
text:
Anal and cervical cancers disproportionately affect populations at high risk of poor outcomes.
The proposed SPORE will study these cancers in different population groups through transformative, community-engaged translational research and career enhancement activities.

title: Extrachromosomal DNA as a driver of heterogeneity and plasticity in glioblastoma
text:
Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most common primary brain tumor, and the inability to improve its median
overall survival (~14 months) is thought to be due, in part, to its hallmark heterogeneity and plasticity. A type or
“class” of amplification called extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) is more prevalent in GBM than any other cancer
type, harbors genes that are known to drive transcriptionally-defined cellular states, and promotes high cell-to-
cell variation of oncogene copy number due to its nonequal segregation during cell division. This application
investigates whether ecDNA enables the characteristic heterogeneity and plasticity of GBM in the context of
tumor initiation and drug resistance.

title: Structure-guided approaches to prevent polymyxin-induced acute kidney injury
text:
Polymyxin is a last-line antibiotic for multi-drug resistant infections, but its use is limited by renal
toxicity mediated by its uptake into the proximal tubules of the kidney by the receptor, LRP2.
The interaction of LRP2 with polymyxin will be characterized with structural methods. This
structural data will be used to design inhibitors of the LRP2-polymyxin interaction that could
protect the kidney.

title: Exosome Secretion in Tumor Aggressiveness
text:
This proposed research is to investigate the role of exosomes in cancer cell adhesion and migration, and
extracellular matrix assembly, which are key events in cancer metastasis and tumor microenvironment
maintenance. We will use a novel in vitro assay developed in the laboratory and state-of-the-art imaging
techniques to determine the impact of exosome secretion from cancer cells as well as fibroblasts. This project
is relevant to public health because it will lead to a greater understanding of the role of exosome secretion in
tumor aggressiveness.

title: EvolvingSTEM: a classroom research curriculum in microbiology that helps students see themselves as scientists
text: The EvolvingSTEM program will use a research-education partnership to educate high school introductory biology students about evolutionary biology, microbiology, and their impact on human health using authentic experimentation and 21st century bioinformatic skills. Our program increases understanding of these topics and their connection to biomedical advances and public health. Our program will improve design and implementation of research experiences that involve high school students in research methods and concepts that are rarely available in conventional classroom activities, and will determine which interventions (e.g., near-peer mentorship, student-driven inquiry) lead to sustained engagement in STEM and pursuit of STEM-related careers.

title: Nutritional landscape and community interactions in the vaginal microbiome
text:
The vaginal mucosa is a complex and understudied ecosystem. Despite the importance of the vaginal microbiota
on reproductive health, the fundamental principles that govern microbial interactions and persistent colonization
remain largely unknown. We will define the nutritional landscape and characterize the impact of nutrient
acquisition and exchange on community dynamics during bacterial colonization and persistence within the
vaginal mucosa.

title: Cross Scale Interrogation of NPD Genes (SING) in mice
text:
Human genetic studies identified hundreds of different risk genes associated with Neurodevelopmental and
psychiatric disorders (NPDs). Here, we propose to establish an Assay and Data Generation Center (ADGCs) to
systematically examine altered molecular, cellular, neural circuits, and behavior by loss of NPD genes in mice.
Our data will help to unveil crucial biological pathways to explain NPDs, which can inform future therapeutic
approaches.

title: Duke PRIME Cancer Research Program
text: Innovations in cancer prevention, treatment, and cure are at risk because an insufficient number of people are entering and persisting in the biomedical research workforce. To address this, we have launched the Duke Preparing Research scholars In bioMEdical sciences (PRIME): Cancer Research Program, a sustainable program that will develop pathways in academic careers and enhance their success by providing early exposure to cancer research experiences, mentorship, skills-building, and scientific networks. This program will recruit and prepare the next generation of scientists to advance cancer care and will serve as a model for expanding across disciplines to develop the biomedical workforce and meet the nation’s needs for innovation in medicine.

title: Investigating the Impact of Adolescent Intermittent Ethanol on GLP-1R function in Central Amygdala
text:
Adolescent alcohol exposure significantly increases risk for developing alcohol use disorder (AUD) in
adulthood, yet the neurobiological mechanisms underlying this vulnerability are poorly understood. This project
will determine how adolescent alcohol exposure disrupts glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) signaling
in amygdala microcircuitry, which regulates negative affect and alcohol-seeking behaviors, using an integrated
approach combining electrophysiology, transcriptional profiling, and functional connectivity mapping. These
findings will inform how patients with adolescent alcohol history may respond when prescribed GLP-1R
agonists, which are increasingly used clinically for metabolic disorders and which show promise as a novel
AUD therapeutic.

title: Personalized sepsis-risk engine using explainable AI and in vitro validation
text:
Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia thrusts cancer patients into a uniquely vulnerable state where infections
rapidly evolve into fatal sepsis, now responsible > 30% of intensive-care admissions, > 2-fold increase in
mortality, and an estimated mean cost of > $45,000 per admission for cancer patients. Our research aims to
elucidate the dynamic, systems-level host responses that precipitate abrupt decompensation, creating a critical
opportunity to build mechanistic, patient-specific models that can forecast sepsis infection and ultimately
enabling personalizing treatments to improve human health. By leveraging multi-modal data, machine learning,
mathematical modeling, and in vitro culture systems, we seek to understand how the host environment reshapes
cellular phenotypes and turn those insights into dynamic, patient‑specific predictions for sepsis, which aligns with
the NIGMS mission by advancing the fundamental understanding of biological processes and developing
innovative, cost-effective tools leveraging human-based research technologies to enhance treatment strategies
for sepsis.

title: Alveolar responses to viral lung infection
text:
Viral lung infection is a major cause of severe lung injury and death. This proposal aims to gain new
understanding of how viruses, specifically influenza, cause lung injury, with the overall goal of identifying new
treatment approaches that decrease lung injury and increase survival. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and
threat of future pandemics by other viruses, including influenza, give special importance to this research.

title: Characterizing the Genetic Risk for Alzheimer Disease in African and Admixed African-American Ancestries
text: This project will provide whole genome sequencing (8,100), Alzheimer's disease (AD) plasma biomarkers (7,500), and cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk biomarker data (9,000) on African and African American individuals ascertained as part of the READD-ADSP U19. We will also collect longitudinal clinical and plasma biomarker data by recontacting and performing follow-up visits after ~4 years with cognitively intact and mild cognitively impaired individuals from this cohort. Analysis of this data will allow identification of rare genetic variants contributing to AD risk and protection and include biomarker and CVD markers in these models. This will add to this invaluable resource for the Alzheimer's disease (AD) research community to enhance efforts to discover targets for AD diagnosis, prevention, and treatment that apply to individuals of all ancestral backgrounds.
